newsitem.title: JAPAN: Zinc - Japan low-grade prices ease, high-grade tight.
newsitem.headline: Zinc - Japan low-grade prices ease, high-grade tight.

text.p: Zinc exports from China and North Korea have created an oversupply of low-grade metal in Japan, although high-grade zinc prices continue surging amid tight supplies, traders said on Monday.

"The (zinc) market is now completely divided. The prices for Special High Grade (SHG) metal and Special High (SH) are far apart," said one trader. "We've never seen this before, but it's going to stay like this for a while."

Traders said Japan's premiums for SHG material were high at $50 to $100 per tonne over London Metal Exchange (LME) cash prices, as China was delivering the metal to the LME warehouse in Singapore to cover short positions rather than exporting to Japan or other nations.

Lower grade materials, on the other hand, are being offered at a discount of up to $100 under LME cash prices, as China and North Korea boost exports to take advantage of rallying prices on the LME, they said.

"It's very difficult to come by SHG zinc. They say it's sold out up to September and October," said another trader. "Some users are now mixing low-grade metal into SHG metal to cut costs, although the number of users who can do that is very limited."

The drying up of Chinese offers for SHG zinc, attributed to the need to cover LME short positions taken at prices around $1,100 per tonne earlier this year, occurred at a time when Japan had just about used up the metal imported in April under a once-a-year tariff exemption scheme, traders said.

Although Japan's SHG zinc imports under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) on April 1 this year were heavy at more than 110,000 tonnes, strong demand for galvanised steel sheet fuelled a surge in Japanese zinc consumption, they said.

"Steelmakers are faring well. The third quarter looks as good as the previous one," said a trader at one of Japan's major non-ferrous metal smelters. "Maybe it (galvanised steel production) is too much. We might see an adjustment after October, although I don't expect a slump."

Some traders are now worried that talks with China on GSP zinc imports for next April may not start in October, as originally planned. At the same time, however, many are also cautious about Japanese demand later this year due to declining car exports and the currency crisis in Southeast Asia.
"People are sceptical whether China will really deliver the metal, although there's plenty of zinc in the LME warehouse in Singapore," said the trader at a smelter.
Another trader at a trade house said: "There may be a fierce fight over the metal."

In the low-grade zinc market offers remained abundant, as famine-stricken North Korea launched an export drive after international aid allowed it to sell more of the metal directly rather than having to barter it for food, traders said.

Some estimated North Korean exports at a total of 1,500 tonnes over the past two months, or nearly double the rate of 414 tonnes per month in May and June. During the country's absence from the market over the past few years, however, China has been able to expand its Japanese market share.

"North Korea is a bit of an outsider. Although their prices are attractive, delivery and quality are problematic," said the first trader, adding that North Korean metal is often about $50 a tonne cheaper than its Chinese equivalent.
The trader also said that, despite the low prices, he was now reluctant to take low-grade metal due to the wide backwardation on the LME.

Traders agreed the combination of tight SHG supplies and over-abundant SH zinc was likely to last for the rest of the year, as they believed China had not yet finished covering its LME short positions. In July, China said the positions totalled as much as 250,000 tonnes.
